State-dependent baseline models

Kyungsub Lee

2026-10-20

Source: vignettes/articles/state-dependent-baseline.Rmd
state-dependent-baseline.Rmd

These examples reconstruct the current state from event counts and use it in the baseline function mu. Fosset’s spread model disables narrowing at the minimum spread; the queue model makes departures proportional to the number of visitors present. Each model defines its own specification and simulated data.

See the examples overview for other model topics.

library(emhawkes)

Fosset’s state-dependent spread model

Fosset, Bouchaud and Benzaquen (2020), Endogenous Liquidity Crises, Section 4.1, equations (8a)–(8b), model spread widening and narrowing as two event types. Let N+N_+ and N−N_- count these events and let the spread, in ticks, be

S(t)=S0+N+(t)−N−(t). S(t) = S_0 + N_+(t) - N_-(t).

Their linear model has predictable intensities

λ+(t)=ν++a∫[0,t)be−b(t−s)dN+(s),λ−(t)=ν−𝟏{S(t−)≥2}. \lambda_+(t) = \nu_+ + a\int_{[0,t)} b e^{-b(t-s)}\,dN_+(s), \qquad \lambda_-(t) = \nu_-\,\mathbf{1}_{\{S(t-)\ge 2\}}.

Only widening events excite future widening. Narrowing is disabled at a one-tick spread. We use ν+,ν−\nu_+,\nu_- for the paper’s λ0+,λ0−\lambda_0^+,\lambda_0^- and a,ba,b for its α,β\alpha,\beta. The package’s alpha[1, 1] is therefore abab; aa is the integrated excitation, not the jump size. The other alpha entries are fixed zeros. Both event types have unit marks.

The example uses positive rates, 0<a<10<a<1, and an explicit zero initial excitation. This restricts the example to a Hawkes-stable widening process. A stationary spread additionally requires ν+/(1−a)<ν−\nu_+/(1-a)<\nu_-. The values below are chosen for a stationary-spread illustration. The nonlinear models later in the paper are separate specifications.

Define mu, alpha, and beta directly, then construct the hspec object. Rows identify affected event types, and columns identify triggering event types. Log rates enforce positivity, and a logit parameter enforces 0<a<10<a<1. The shared name log_b keeps the same decay parameter in alpha and beta.

spread0_fosset <- 1

mu <- function(param = c(log_nu_plus = log(1), log_nu_minus = log(3)), n, N) {
  previous_event <- max(1L, n - 1L)
  spread <- spread0_fosset + N[previous_event, 1] - N[previous_event, 2]
  matrix(c(exp(param[["log_nu_plus"]]),
    exp(param[["log_nu_minus"]]) * (spread >= 2)), nrow = 2)
}

alpha <- function(param = c(logit_a = qlogis(0.4), log_b = log(2))) {
  jumps <- matrix(0, nrow = 2, ncol = 2)
  jumps[1, 1] <- plogis(param[["logit_a"]]) * exp(param[["log_b"]])
  jumps
}

beta <- function(param = c(log_b = log(2))) {
  matrix(exp(param[["log_b"]]), nrow = 2, ncol = 2)
}

h_fosset <- new("hspec", mu = mu, alpha = alpha, beta = beta)

For the baseline callback, N[n - 1, ] describes the state before event n. The same callback is called with n + 1 after the jump, so the narrowing rate changes immediately when the spread reaches or leaves one tick.

set.seed(20261018)
path_fosset <- hsim(h_fosset, size = 4001, lambda_component0 = 0)
spread_fosset <- spread0_fosset + path_fosset$N[, 1] - path_fosset$N[, 2]
stopifnot(all(spread_fosset >= 1),
  all(path_fosset$lambda[c(spread0_fosset, head(spread_fosset, -1)) == 1, 2] == 0),
  all(path_fosset$rambda[spread_fosset == 1, 2] == 0))
plot(path_fosset$arrival, spread_fosset, type = "s",
  xlab = "Time", ylab = "Spread (ticks)")

Estimate all four model parameters from a different starting point. The example uses R’s stats optimizer and the default numerical gradient. Automatic engine selection uses the supported C++ likelihood; simulation of this count-dependent baseline uses the R path. No analytic Jacobians are required. Change the default param vectors to choose fitting starting values, then create a second hspec.

formals(mu)$param <- c(log_nu_plus = log(0.7), log_nu_minus = log(2.5))
formals(alpha)$param <- c(logit_a = qlogis(0.25), log_b = log(1.2))
formals(beta)$param <- c(log_b = log(1.2))
start_fosset <- new("hspec", mu = mu, alpha = alpha, beta = beta)
fit_fosset <- hfit(start_fosset,
  inter_arrival = path_fosset$inter_arrival, type = path_fosset$type,
  lambda_component0 = 0, optimizer = "stats", method = "BFGS",
  control = list(maxit = 500, reltol = 1e-10))
theta_fosset <- coef(fit_fosset)
estimated_fosset <- c(
  nu_plus = exp(theta_fosset[["log_nu_plus"]]),
  nu_minus = exp(theta_fosset[["log_nu_minus"]]),
  a = plogis(theta_fosset[["logit_a"]]),
  b = exp(theta_fosset[["log_b"]]))
cbind(true = c(nu_plus = 1, nu_minus = 3, a = 0.4, b = 2),
  estimated = estimated_fosset)
#>          true estimated
#> nu_plus   1.0 0.9811201
#> nu_minus  3.0 3.0865001
#> a         0.4 0.4240015
#> b         2.0 1.7920735
fit_diagnostics(fit_fosset)$status
#> [1] "ok"
fit_diagnostics(fit_fosset)$computation$engine
#> $requested
#> [1] "auto"
#> 
#> $used
#> [1] "cpp"
#> 
#> $fallback_reason
#> NULL

The estimated coefficients are on the log/logit scale. Parameter recovery varies between realizations; inspect convergence and uncertainty rather than expecting exact recovery from a single path.

There is an independent check for the narrowing rate. If TopenT_{\mathrm{open}} is the time spent with S≥2S\ge2, its log-likelihood contribution is N−(T)log⁡ν−−ν−TopenN_-(T)\log\nu_- - \nu_- T_{\mathrm{open}}. Its maximum is ν̂−=N−(T)/Topen\widehat{\nu}_- = N_-(T)/T_{\mathrm{open}}. The observation window ends at the last supplied event.

open_time_fosset <- sum(path_fosset$inter_arrival[-1] *
  (head(spread_fosset, -1) >= 2))
c(fitted = estimated_fosset[["nu_minus"]],
  independent = sum(path_fosset$type == 2) / open_time_fosset)
#>      fitted independent 
#>      3.0865      3.0865
restored_fosset <- fitted_hspec(fit_fosset)
replay_fosset <- do.call(logLik, c(list(object = restored_fosset,
  inter_arrival = path_fosset$inter_arrival, type = path_fosset$type,
  infer = TRUE), fit_initial_state(fit_fosset)))
stopifnot(isTRUE(all.equal(as.numeric(logLik(fit_fosset)),
  unname(replay_fosset$loglikelihood), tolerance = 1e-8)))

A Hawkes/M/infinity queue: website visits and departures

Daw and Pender (2018), Queues Driven by Hawkes Processes, Section 3, define a Hawkes/PH/infinity queue. With one exponential service phase, their model is a Hawkes/M/infinity queue. Interpret arrivals as website visits and service completions as departures. Every visitor starts service immediately; Q(t)Q(t) counts all visitors still present in the system.

Let NinN_{\mathrm{in}} and NoutN_{\mathrm{out}} count visits and departures. With initial population Q0Q_0 and zero initial excitation, the model is

Q(t)=Q0+Nin(t)−Nout(t), Q(t) = Q_0 + N_{\mathrm{in}}(t) - N_{\mathrm{out}}(t),

λin(t)=ν+a∫[0,t)e−b(t−s)dNin(s),λout(t)=δQ(t−). \lambda_{\mathrm{in}}(t) = \nu + a\int_{[0,t)} e^{-b(t-s)}\,dN_{\mathrm{in}}(s), \qquad \lambda_{\mathrm{out}}(t) = \delta Q(t-).

Here ν\nu is the arrival baseline, aa is the jump in arrival intensity, bb is its decay rate, and 1/δ1/\delta is the mean service time. In the paper’s notation, these are λ*\lambda^*, α\alpha, β\beta, and the single-phase service rate. Unlike the normalized kernel in the preceding spread example, this kernel has jump size aa and integrated excitation a/ba/b.

The arrival process is an autonomous Hawkes process. The population affects the departure intensity, while an arrival’s contribution to future arrivals continues to decay after that visitor leaves. This is exactly the single-phase special case of the paper’s queueing model.

Define the three components and construct the hspec object directly. Log parameters keep all four rates positive, and the function-valued alpha keeps its three structural zeros fixed during estimation. The example uses a<ba<b for a stable arrival process; the log parameterization alone does not enforce that inequality.

q0_queue <- 0

mu <- function(param = c(log_nu = log(0.4), log_delta = log(0.8)), n, N) {
  previous_event <- max(1L, n - 1L)
  population <- q0_queue + N[previous_event, 1] - N[previous_event, 2]
  matrix(c(exp(param[["log_nu"]]),
    exp(param[["log_delta"]]) * population), nrow = 2)
}

alpha <- function(param = c(log_a = log(0.5))) {
  jumps <- matrix(0, nrow = 2, ncol = 2)
  jumps[1, 1] <- exp(param[["log_a"]])
  jumps
}

beta <- function(param = c(log_b = log(1.2))) {
  matrix(exp(param[["log_b"]]), nrow = 2, ncol = 2)
}

h_queue <- new("hspec", mu = mu, alpha = alpha, beta = beta)

Event type 1 is a visit and event type 2 is a departure. The baseline callback reads N[n - 1, ] to obtain the population before event n. After the event it is called with n + 1, so the departure rate changes immediately. When Q=0Q=0, the departure rate is zero without a separate boundary correction.

set.seed(884102)
path_queue <- hsim(h_queue, size = 6001, lambda_component0 = 0)
population_queue <- q0_queue + path_queue$N[, 1] - path_queue$N[, 2]
population_before_queue <- c(q0_queue, head(population_queue, -1))
stopifnot(all(population_queue >= 0),
  all(population_before_queue[path_queue$type == 2] > 0),
  all(path_queue$rambda[population_queue == 0, 2] == 0))

For a readable view, plot the first 400 events. rambda contains the intensity immediately after each event, so its second column equals δQ(t)\delta Q(t).

local({
  old_par <- par(mfrow = c(2, 1), mar = c(4, 4, 1, 1), mgp = c(2.5, 0.8, 0))
  on.exit(par(old_par))
  shown <- seq_len(min(401L, length(path_queue$arrival)))
  plot(path_queue$arrival[shown], population_queue[shown], type = "s",
    xlab = "Time", ylab = "Visitors present")
  plot(path_queue$arrival[shown], path_queue$rambda[shown, 2], type = "s",
    xlab = "Time", ylab = "Departure intensity")
})

Estimate the four rates from both arrival and departure times. This uses the stats optimizer with numerical differentiation. Simulation uses the R event loop for the state-dependent baseline; automatic likelihood selection supports the C++ engine for this observed-count callback.

formals(mu)$param <- c(log_nu = log(0.3), log_delta = log(1.1))
formals(alpha)$param <- c(log_a = log(0.3))
formals(beta)$param <- c(log_b = log(0.9))
start_queue <- new("hspec", mu = mu, alpha = alpha, beta = beta)
fit_queue <- hfit(start_queue,
  inter_arrival = path_queue$inter_arrival, type = path_queue$type,
  lambda_component0 = 0, optimizer = "stats", method = "BFGS",
  control = list(maxit = 500, reltol = 1e-10))
theta_queue <- coef(fit_queue)
estimated_queue <- c(
  nu = exp(theta_queue[["log_nu"]]),
  delta = exp(theta_queue[["log_delta"]]),
  a = exp(theta_queue[["log_a"]]),
  b = exp(theta_queue[["log_b"]]))
cbind(true = c(nu = 0.4, delta = 0.8, a = 0.5, b = 1.2),
  estimated = estimated_queue)
#>       true estimated
#> nu     0.4 0.3919561
#> delta  0.8 0.8117900
#> a      0.5 0.5657843
#> b      1.2 1.3811091
fit_diagnostics(fit_queue)$status
#> [1] "ok"

The likelihood factorizes into an arrival contribution and a departure contribution. Over the observation window ending at the last supplied event, the latter is, up to parameter-independent terms,

Nout(T)log⁡δ−δ∫0TQ(t)dt. N_{\mathrm{out}}(T)\log\delta - \delta\int_0^T Q(t)\,dt.

Thus δ̂=Nout(T)/∫0TQ(t)dt\widehat\delta=N_{\mathrm{out}}(T)/\int_0^T Q(t)\,dt provides an independent check of the fitted service rate. Restore the fitted specification and replay the same data to check that its likelihood is preserved.

person_time_queue <- sum(path_queue$inter_arrival[-1] * head(population_queue, -1))
c(fitted = estimated_queue[["delta"]],
  independent = sum(path_queue$type == 2) / person_time_queue)
#>      fitted independent 
#>   0.8117900   0.8117901
restored_queue <- fitted_hspec(fit_queue)
replay_queue <- do.call(logLik, c(list(object = restored_queue,
  inter_arrival = path_queue$inter_arrival, type = path_queue$type,
  infer = TRUE), fit_initial_state(fit_queue)))
stopifnot(isTRUE(all.equal(as.numeric(logLik(fit_queue)),
  unname(replay_queue$loglikelihood), tolerance = 1e-8)))

This example starts with q0_queue = 0. For a nonempty initial system, set q0_queue before defining mu and keep it fixed through simulation and fitting. Initial population and initial Hawkes excitation are distinct: q0_queue counts visitors already present, while lambda_component0 describes the remaining excitation from arrivals before the observation window.
